newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: FEATURE - Slovenia gambles by blocking foreign money.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Slovenia gambles by blocking foreign money.

text.p: Slovenia, the northernmost and richest of the former Yugoslav republics, has performed well since throwing off communism but risks recession unless it dismantles barriers to foreign investment.

Analysts believe economic growth could slow, boosting already high unemployment, unless foreigners are given a freer hand to invest. The current reluctance to let in foreign capitalists is also threatening Slovenia's drive to join the European Union.
"Without an in-flow of fresh capital, Slovenia could be facing recession and higher joblessness," said Franci Krizanic, economist at Ljubljana University.
Slovenian economic growth eased to 3.5 percent last year from 3.9 percent in 1995 and 5.3 percent in 1994. Unemployment was 14.4 percent in December against 14 percent the previous month.

Krizanic said one of the most pressing tasks for Slovenia's new government, a broad coalition formed last month, was to allow foreign funds to flow freely into the country in order to reduce borrowing costs for domestic firms.
"That would make capital more accessible to Slovenian companies," he said.

High interest rates, which incorporate high inflation and change monthly, make it difficult for companies to raise capital. January average short term nominal interest rates were 18.1 percent compared with 23.1 percent a year ago.
Foreign inflows would increase the supply of capital and reduce the cost of money to domestic companies.
GOVERNMENT ADMITS GROWTH HINGES ON FOREIGN INVESTMENT
In a sign of his willingness to listen to such advice, Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek conceded that future healthy economic growth would hinge on foreign investment.

"Fast development requires a lot of capital and we do not have it. The prevailing attitude towards foreign investment is fairly negative and that is restricting development," Drnovsek, leader of the centre-left Liberal Democrats, said in a newspaper interview.
The government is aiming for four percent economic growth this year against a backdrop of steady employment and inflation.

Marjan Svetlicic, economics professor at Ljubljana University, believes Drnovsek will strive to end a deeply entrenched distrust of foreigners, linked to the newly-found sense of national identity after independence from Yugoslavia.
"There is a general fear of foreigners in Slovenia. Most people have not yet realised that globalisation can increase a country's sovereignty rather than decrease it," Svetlicic said.
Theoretically, companies could issue eurobonds to raise capital, but there is no detailed legislation regarding issuance and the process would be too complex for many.
Domestic companies may borrow overseas, but having to deposit 40 percent at the central bank, if the loan is for less than five years, defeats the whole purpose, economists say.
NEW CENTRAL BANK RULES STIFLE INFLOW OF FOREIGN MONEY
Direct foreign investment last year was steady at an estimated $176 million.

Foreign inflows in Slovenian securities, in contrast, was booming at the start of this year until the central bank imposed new restrictions on foreign funds. In the first six weeks of 1997 portfolio funds invested $30 million -- almost half of their total investment last year.
On February 11 the Bank of Slovenia ruled that international investors could trade only through special accounts at one of the country's 14 fully licensed banks.
These banks have signalled they may charge as much as 12 percent in handling fees when the accounts begin operating later this month.
"As a result of this ruling the stock market is dead," said Toni Apollonio, an analyst at A banka bank.

Overseas investors may buy stakes in most companies. But they are not normally allowed to participate in new share issues. In addition, the central bank has to approve foreign purchases of shares in any Slovenian bank.
PRIVATISATION SHOULD BE OPEN TO FOREIGNERS
Accommodating foreign participation in privatisation would help to ease demand for money for modernisation and expansion, economists say.
Accelerated privatisation programmes would also go a long way towards beating off recession and promoting economic growth.

Slovenia began the privatisation of some 1,500 companies in early 1994. To date, 931 are in private hands and 430 are mid-way through the process. The sale of the remainder is expected to be completed by end-1997.
No decision regarding two of the three largest Slovenian banks still in government hands has been taken.
Neither does a blueprint exist for the privatisation of strategic industries such as railways, steel, or telecommunications.
BETTER ATTITUDE TO FOREIGNERS WILL HELP EU AMBITIONS

Economists forecast that politicians and the central bank would have to adopt a more liberal stance, however, if Slovenia was serious in its bid to join the EU. It has already signed an association agreement with the bloc and parliament is due to ratify it in June.
"Slovenia will have to detail its investment legislation and simplify its administrative procedures," said Peter Stanovnik, head of Ljubljana's Institute for Economic Research.

"The ratification of the EU association agreement will probably make the biggest contribution to improving the climate for foreign investment. It will push Slovenia further towards European standards," Svetlicic agreed.
Analysts said it was too soon to predict the effectiveness of Drnovsek's new government but they noted the Liberal Democrats had maintained their grip on key foreign and finance ministries.
Drnovsek has served as prime minister since April 1993. His latest team combines the Liberal Democrats, the conservative People's Party and the pensioners' party Desus.
"The new government is very strong and should therefore be capable of enforcing the necessary changes," Krizanic said.
